slides.title: Mid-latitude (extratropical) cyclones
slides.body:
Mid-latitude cyclones are low-pressure systems forming along polar front + driven by baroclinic instability:

• **Genesis**: perturbation along front; baroclinic instability amplifies; cyclone develops.
• **Mature structure**: central low (~970-1000 hPa); rotation counterclockwise (NH); diameter 1000-3000 km.
• **Fronts**: warm front advances + lifts warm air over cold; cold front follows + lifts warm air abruptly. Occluded front when cold front catches warm front.
• **Conveyor belts**: warm conveyor (ascending warm-sector air, source of heavy precip); cold conveyor (low-level cold air east of low); dry intrusion from stratosphere descending behind cold front.

**Lifecycle** (Norwegian Cyclone Model, Bjerknes 1922):
1. Initial wave on front.
2. Open wave (developing low + frontal structure).
3. Mature cyclone (deepest + occlusion forming).
4. Decaying cyclone (cut-off; decoupling from front).
5. ~3-7 day total lifetime.

**Famous storms**:
- 'Storm of the Century' Mar 1993: NA blizzard, $7B damage.
- Great Storm of 1987 UK: 90+ mph winds; ~18 dead.
- Lothar + Martin Dec 1999 (Europe): record-breaking; 90+ dead.
- Sandy 2012 (hybrid tropical-extratropical): NYC + NJ devastation.

**Bomb cyclones**: rapid intensification (pressure drop > 24 hPa / 24 hr at 60°N). Particularly intense.

**NW Atlantic + Pacific storm tracks**: peak cyclone-genesis regions due to land-sea T contrast + Gulf Stream + Kuroshio heat.

slides.title: Tropical cyclones: hurricanes + typhoons
slides.body:
**Tropical cyclones** (hurricanes = Atlantic + E. Pacific; typhoons = W. Pacific; cyclones = Indian Ocean/Australia) are warm-core, deep-convective systems powered by latent heat of ocean evaporation.

**Formation requirements** (Gray 1968):
1. Warm SST > 26.5 °C (deep mixed layer to ~50 m).
2. Tropical latitudes (>5° from equator for Coriolis but not too high).
3. Pre-existing disturbance (tropical wave from Africa, monsoon trough).
4. Low vertical wind shear (<20 kt or so).
5. Mid-tropospheric humidity (no dry intrusion to kill convection).
6. Conditional instability + sufficient ITCZ moisture.

**Structure** (mature cyclone):
• **Eye**: clear central calm (~30-60 km diameter). Subsiding air. Lowest pressure.
• **Eyewall**: strongest winds (90-300+ km/h); ring of intense convection around eye.
• **Rainbands**: spiral arms of convection, hundreds of km out.
• **Outflow**: at upper troposphere; flows outward from cyclone top.

**Saffir-Simpson scale** (Atlantic):
- Cat 1: 119-153 km/h (74-95 mph)
- Cat 2: 154-177 km/h
- Cat 3: 178-208 km/h (major hurricane)
- Cat 4: 209-251 km/h
- Cat 5: ≥252 km/h

**Recent major events**:
- Patricia 2015: 345 km/h, lowest Atlantic pressure on record (872 hPa).
- Yutu 2018 (W. Pacific): Cat 5, Saipan devastation.
- Dorian 2019 Bahamas: 295 km/h, $7B damage.
- Typhoon Goni Oct 2020: 315 km/h, strongest at landfall.
- Ida 2021: $75B damage.
- Ian 2022: $112B damage.

**Climate change + tropical cyclones**: 
- Frequency: ambiguous trend.
- Intensity: higher fraction of major (Cat 4-5) storms; observed + projected.
- Rapid intensification: ~50% more rapid intensifications since 1980s.
- Slower forward motion: more time over land → more rainfall.
- Storm-surge + flooding worsened by SLR + heavier precipitation.

slides.title: Forecasting + the prediction limits
slides.body:
**Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP)** is the core technology:
- Discretize atmosphere on global grid (~10-25 km horizontal, ~50-100 vertical levels).
- Initial conditions from observations (radiosondes, satellites, aircraft, surface stations, buoys).
- Integrate Navier-Stokes + thermodynamics + radiation + moist physics forward in time.
- Run multiple times with perturbed initial conditions → ensemble forecasts.

**Leading global models**:
- ECMWF IFS: best medium-range skill, ~10-day useful forecast.
- NOAA GFS: free + widely used; ~7-day skill.
- NCEP NAEFS, Météo-France ARPEGE, UK Met UM, JMA GSM.

**ML-based forecasting** (2022-onwards):
- Google DeepMind GraphCast (2022): graph neural network. Beats ECMWF on most metrics at ~1000× less compute.
- Microsoft ClimaX, Aurora; NVIDIA FourCastNet, GenCast (2023, diffusion-based ensemble).
- Pangu-Weather (Huawei 2023): 3D transformer.
- Generating realistic ensembles, calibrated probabilistic forecasts.

**Forecast skill horizon**:
- ~6-hr nowcast: very high skill (radar + satellite + ML).
- 1-3 day: high skill (~95% useful).
- 5-7 day: moderate skill (~70-80%).
- 10-day: marginal skill.
- Beyond 10-14 days: chaos limits deterministic forecasting (Lorenz 1963); only ensemble/statistical skill.

**S2S (subseasonal-to-seasonal)** forecasts (2 weeks - 3 months): emerging area; ENSO + MJO + soil-moisture + sea-ice memory provide some skill.

**Climate vs weather**: weather forecasts deterministic + chaos-limited. Climate prediction is statistical + boundary-condition-driven (different problem). Can predict climate decades ahead with skill; can't predict daily weather more than ~2 weeks.

question.question: Compute the warm-front advance time
question.goal: A warm front extends NW-SE across the central US at 30 °C ahead + 5 °C behind. Wind component perpendicular to front ahead is 30 km/h southward. How long until the warm air mass arrives at a station 100 km north of the current front position?

steps.reveal: 30 km/h. Warm air mass advances at this speed.
100 km / 30 km/h = 3.33 hours. Warm air arrives ~3:20 hr later. Typical mid-lat cyclone warm-front passage timescales.

steps.prompt: Expected temperature change at the station?
steps.reveal: Station temperature rises from 5 °C (behind front, cold) to 30 °C (ahead of front, warm) — 25 °C rise. Likely cloud cover + light rain on warm-front passage; then sunshine in warm sector.

steps.prompt: What weather precedes a warm front?
hints: Warm air lifts gradually over cold.
steps.reveal: Warm air ahead of warm front lifts gradually (gentle slope ~1/200) over cold air. Sequence: high cirrus + cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus → light steady precipitation. Tens of hours of approach. Distinguishes from cold front (steep slope ~1/50; abrupt; squall lines; thunderstorms). Mid-lat winter cyclone warm-front signature is a textbook day-long progressive forecast.

question.question: Classify each weather phenomenon by its formation mechanism.
question.explanation:
Atmospheric phenomena fall into broad classes by formation mechanism:
• **Tropical cyclones** (hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones): warm-core systems fueled by latent heat of ocean evaporation over warm waters (>26.5 °C). Need low vertical wind shear; tropical/subtropical latitudes.
• **Extratropical cyclones**: cold-core systems driven by baroclinic instability along polar front. Strong horizontal T gradient → APE → eddy growth. Mid-latitudes; year-round but stronger in winter.
• **Mesoscale convective systems (MCS)**: organized thunderstorms — supercells, squall lines, derechos. Driven by convective instability + organized dynamics on ~100-500 km scales. Summer-dominant.
• **Frontal weather**: precipitation + wind shifts associated with passage of air-mass boundaries. Often embedded in cyclones; can occur independently. Warm-front: gradual rise + stratiform precip. Cold-front: abrupt rise + convective precip.

Most severe weather involves combinations — e.g., a mid-latitude cyclone has frontal precipitation embedded + may include mesoscale convective elements.

question.question: Why has rapid intensification of tropical cyclones (rapid increase in wind speed over short time) become more frequent since 1980?
options: Warmer ocean surfaces provide more latent heat for storm intensification. Subsurface ocean heat (down to ~100 m) also warming, reducing 'cool-water brake' that previously slowed storms. Combined with often-low wind shear in late-season tropical conditions, storms can intensify rapidly (e.g., from Cat 1 to Cat 5 in 24-36 hr). Increases storm-surge + wind damage; complicates forecasting + evacuation planning. Observed in Atlantic + Pacific basins since 1980s.
question.explanation:
**Rapid intensification (RI)** is defined as wind-speed increase of ≥35 mph (56 km/h) in 24 hours.

**Observed trends (Bhatia+ 2019, Wang+ 2022)**:
- Probability of RI has increased ~50% since 1980s.
- More common in late season (Aug-Oct in Atlantic).
- More common where ocean heat content extends deeper.
- Patricia 2015 (E. Pacific): 100 mph wind increase in 24 hr — record.
- Ian 2022 (Gulf of Mexico): 70 mph in 24 hr; ~$112B damage in Florida.

**Physical mechanism**:
1. **Warm surface water** (>28-29 °C) provides energy via evaporation. Latent heat → eyewall convection.
2. **Deep warm layer** (mixed layer + thermocline below): if upper ocean is uniformly warm to ~50-100 m, storm-induced upwelling doesn't cool surface much. 'Loop currents' (Gulf of Mexico) or 'rings' (Atlantic) of unusually warm + deep water are RI hotspots.
3. **Low wind shear**: vertical shear of horizontal winds disrupts vertical cyclone structure. Calm shear allows tight, organized circulation to intensify.
4. **High humidity**: aircraft-measured pre-storm humidity correlates with RI likelihood.
5. **Inner-core processes**: eyewall replacement cycles, convective bursts, can trigger sudden deepening.

**Climate change linkages**:
- SST warming: tropical Atlantic SST risen ~1 °C since 1950s.
- Ocean heat content (OHC): increasing globally, especially in subtropics.
- 26.5 °C isotherm: pushed deeper (>50 m typical now in late-season Atlantic).
- Combined: more RI 'fuel' available.

**Forecasting challenge**:
- RI is the hardest aspect of TC forecasting. Models systematically under-predict RI events.
- Aircraft observations (Hurricane Hunters reconnaissance) critical.
- Recent advances: ML-based RI prediction (NHC adopted DTOPS + SHIPS-RI models).
- 24-hr RI prediction accuracy has improved but remains <50% in many cases.

**Implications**:
- Less time for evacuation (1-2 days less warning than historical).
- Higher peak intensities at landfall.
- Greater wind + surge + rainfall damage.
- Underestimated by historical-extrapolation insurance + planning models.

Climate-adapted infrastructure + evacuation planning must account for higher RI probability + faster onset of strongest storms.

hints: What's the role of ocean heat?
slides.workedSolution: Rapid intensification: ≥35 mph wind increase in 24 hr. ~50% more frequent since 1980s. Causes: warmer SSTs (>28-29 °C), deeper warm layer (loop currents, ocean heat content), low wind shear, high humidity. Patricia 2015 (100 mph/24 hr record), Ian 2022 (70 mph/24 hr → $112B). Forecasting challenge: under-predicted by models; aircraft + ML-based methods help. Implications: less evacuation time, higher peak intensities, greater damage. Climate adaptation must account for RI.

question.question: A hurricane with 250 km/h wind has Cat what on Saffir-Simpson scale? (Cat 1: 119-153; Cat 2: 154-177; Cat 3: 178-208; Cat 4: 209-251; Cat 5: ≥252)

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain why modern medium-range weather forecasts (~7 days ahead) are remarkably skillful, while ~14-day forecasts remain marginal.
question.rubric: Mentions: medium-range forecasts (5-10 day) have benefited from: (1) better numerical models (higher resolution, better physics, improved data assimilation); (2) huge observational network (satellites, radiosondes, aircraft, surface stations); (3) ensemble approaches quantifying uncertainty; (4) recent ML-based methods (GraphCast, ECMWF AIFS). Skill: ECMWF medium-range forecast at day-9 today equals day-5 in 1980s. Beyond ~10-14 days, chaos limit (Lorenz 1963) — sensitive dependence on initial conditions means deterministic predictability vanishes. Two close initial states diverge to completely different forecast outcomes over ~weeks. Some signal remains in monthly + seasonal averaged statistics from large-scale boundary conditions (SST, snow cover, ENSO state). Subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) forecasts emerging area; modest skill from MJO + soil moisture + sea ice. Concludes: deterministic limit ~14 days; statistical/seasonal predictability extends much further; ML may close some gap with new methods exploiting boundary-condition memory.
